newsitem.title: USA: Mass. study recommends Turnpike Authority split.
newsitem.headline: Mass. study recommends Turnpike Authority split.

text.p: A legislative study released on Thursday recommends that the Massachusetts Turnpike Authority be split in two and that tolls on Boston Harbor crossings be doubled to help pay the state's share of the $10.4 billion Central Artery/Ted Williams Tunnel project known as the "Big Dig."
The report, prepared by independent consultants, recommends that tolls on the three Boston Harbor crossings, including the Ted Williams Tunnel, be doubled beginning July 1, 1997.
According to the study released by Massachusetts Secretary of Transporation James Kerasiotes, no additional toll hikes would be needed for five years once tolls have been doubled.

The study suggests the use of Grant Anticipation Notes (GANS), as well as toll hikes as a principal financing technique to meet the completion requirements of $150 million to $730 million for the project. It also suggests GANs be used to meet the project's interim cash flow requirements estimated at between $900 million and $1.3 billion, and cumlative operating expense requirement of up to $220 million between 1999 and 2005.

The GANs financing is proposed to address peak period cashflow needs rather than incur additional general obligation debt, the study said. It envisions using GANs to borrow against future federal highway transportation grants. The study suggests splitting the Turnpike Authority into two cost centers.
The western section which would run from Route 128 to the Massachusetts/New York State border would be self-sustaining and without toll adjustments could retire its debt by 2010.
The eastern section would be known as the Massachusetts Highway System (MHS). It would include most, but not all, of the "Big Dig," the nation's largest highway project.

The study recommends that the Turnpike Authority contribute $700 million toward the completion of MHS during peak construction years. It also suggests the Turnpike Authority contribute an additional $300 million at the completion of the nation's largest highway project.
The Massachusetts Highway Department should contribute $25 million annually toward the operation of the Central Artery Project, the study said.
But the level of contributions from MassPort, the authority that operates Logan Airport and which would benefit directly from most of the improvements, have not yet been determined.
